questions.stem: This fundoscopic photograph shows cotton-wool spots, arteriovenous nicking, and flame-shaped retinal hemorrhages around the optic disc. These retinal findings are the classic end-organ manifestation of which systemic condition?

explanation.summary: Arteriovenous nicking, cotton-wool spots (retinal ischemia), and flame hemorrhages reflect chronic hypertensive damage to the retinal arterioles, making the retina a window onto systemic hypertensive vascular injury.
explanation.whyCorrect: Arteriovenous nicking, cotton-wool spots (retinal ischemia), and flame hemorrhages reflect chronic hypertensive damage to the retinal arterioles, making the retina a window onto systemic hypertensive vascular injury.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute angle-closure glaucoma causes a painful red eye with a fixed mid-dilated pupil and corneal edema, not retinal hemorrhages and AV nicking.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Central retinal artery occlusion gives a pale, whitened retina with a cherry-red spot, not AV nicking and flame hemorrhages.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Proliferative diabetic retinopathy shows microaneurysms, dot-blot hemorrhages and new vessels; AV nicking points to hypertensive arteriolar disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Retinal detachment shows an elevated, undulating gray retina with flashes and floaters, not vascular changes around the disc.

questions.stem: These renal biopsy panels from a hypertensive patient show (A) glomeruli and an arteriole with homogeneous pink wall thickening and luminal narrowing, and (B) an arteriole with concentric 'onion-skin' laminated wall thickening. What vascular process do these images depict?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fibromuscular dysplasia of the renal artery

explanation.summary: Chronic hypertension produces hyaline arteriolosclerosis (homogeneous protein deposition in the wall) and, with more severe/malignant hypertension, hyperplastic 'onion-skin' arteriolosclerosis, both narrowing the lumen and driving nephrosclerosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chronic hypertension produces hyaline arteriolosclerosis (homogeneous protein deposition in the wall) and, with more severe/malignant hypertension, hyperplastic 'onion-skin' arteriolosclerosis, both narrowing the lumen and driving nephrosclerosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Polyarteritis nodosa causes transmural necrotizing inflammation of medium arteries with microaneurysms, not hyaline or onion-skin thickening of arterioles.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Amyloid deposits stain with Congo red and expand the mesangium and vessel walls, but they do not form laminated onion-skin layers.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fibromuscular dysplasia affects the main renal artery with a beaded pattern, not small intrarenal arterioles.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Renal cell carcinoma forms a tumor mass of clear or papillary cells, not diffuse thickening of arteriolar walls.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old with new hypertension is found to have renal artery stenosis. On this classification diagram, into which branch does her hypertension fall?

explanation.summary: Secondary hypertension (5-10% of cases) results from an identifiable cause such as renovascular, renal, or endocrine disease; primary hypertension has no identifiable cause.
explanation.whyCorrect: Secondary hypertension (5-10% of cases) results from an identifiable cause such as renovascular, renal, or endocrine disease; primary hypertension has no identifiable cause.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pulmonary arterial hypertension is elevated pressure in the pulmonary circulation, separate from systemic hypertension caused by renal artery disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension is raised CSF pressure, typically in obese young women, unrelated to systemic blood pressure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Primary hypertension has no identifiable cause, so a hypertension explained by renal artery stenosis cannot be primary.
whyWrongByChoice.E: White-coat hypertension is elevated readings only in the clinic with normal out-of-office pressure, not hypertension from a structural lesion.

questions.stem: This hormonal cascade begins with hepatic angiotensinogen and raises blood pressure through vasoconstriction and renal sodium/water reabsorption. What is this system called?

explanation.summary: The diagram depicts the RAAS: renin converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, pulmonary ACE converts it to angiotensin II, which drives vasoconstriction and aldosterone-mediated Na/water retention.
explanation.whyCorrect: The diagram depicts the RAAS: renin converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, pulmonary ACE converts it to angiotensin II, which drives vasoconstriction and aldosterone-mediated Na/water retention.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The kallikrein-kinin system generates bradykinin from kininogen and causes vasodilation, not vasoconstriction from angiotensinogen.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Natriuretic peptides from the heart promote sodium excretion and vasodilation, lowering blood pressure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The baroreflex is a neural arc of stretch receptors and autonomic outflow, not a hormonal cascade starting with a liver protein.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The HPA axis runs from CRH to ACTH to cortisol and does not start with hepatic angiotensinogen.

questions.stem: This schematic shows a renal change leading to increased intravascular volume alongside vasoconstriction, together producing hypertension. Which renal event is depicted as the initiating step?

explanation.summary: Enhanced tubular Na+ reabsorption expands intravascular volume, which combined with vasoconstriction raises the product of SVR and cardiac output, elevating blood pressure.
explanation.whyCorrect: Enhanced tubular Na+ reabsorption expands intravascular volume, which combined with vasoconstriction raises the product of SVR and cardiac output, elevating blood pressure.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Decreased contractility lowers cardiac output and blood pressure; it is not a renal event.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Peripheral vasodilation lowers resistance and pressure, the opposite of the vasoconstriction shown.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Natriuresis with volume loss shrinks intravascular volume and lowers blood pressure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reduced systemic vascular resistance would lower blood pressure, and it is not a renal tubular event.

questions.stem: The arrow on this MR angiogram of the aorta and renal vessels indicates a narrowing that raises blood pressure primarily through which mechanism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increased cardiac output from severe anemia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Direct autonomous aldosterone secretion by an adrenal tumor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Catecholamine surge from an adrenal medullary tumor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Excess cortisol production causing sodium retention

explanation.summary: Reduced perfusion pressure from renal artery stenosis is sensed by the juxtaglomerular apparatus, triggering renin release and downstream angiotensin II/aldosterone activation, which drives renovascular hypertension.
explanation.whyCorrect: Reduced perfusion pressure from renal artery stenosis is sensed by the juxtaglomerular apparatus, triggering renin release and downstream angiotensin II/aldosterone activation, which drives renovascular hypertension.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Severe anemia raises cardiac output but usually lowers resistance and is not caused by a narrowed renal artery.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Autonomous aldosterone secretion is primary hyperaldosteronism from an adrenal adenoma or hyperplasia, with suppressed renin, unlike a renal artery narrowing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A catecholamine surge comes from a pheochromocytoma of the adrenal medulla, not from narrowing of a renal artery.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cortisol excess is Cushing syndrome from pituitary, adrenal or exogenous sources, unrelated to renal artery anatomy.

questions.stem: This renal angiogram shows a beaded 'string of beads' contour of the artery. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: The alternating areas of stenosis and dilation give a classic 'string of beads' pattern on angiography, diagnostic of fibromuscular dysplasia of the renal artery.
explanation.whyCorrect: The alternating areas of stenosis and dilation give a classic 'string of beads' pattern on angiography, diagnostic of fibromuscular dysplasia of the renal artery.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis narrows the ostium or proximal artery in older patients and does not alternate with dilations.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A renal artery aneurysm is a single focal outpouching, not repeated alternating webs and dilations.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Polyarteritis nodosa causes multiple small microaneurysms in intrarenal and mesenteric branches, rather than beading of the mid-to-distal main renal artery.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Takayasu arteritis causes long, smooth stenoses of the aorta and its branch origins in young Asian women, not a beaded pattern.

questions.stem: This figure illustrates a patient with moon facies, buffalo hump, central obesity with abdominal striae, thin skin, proximal muscle weakness, and hypertension from cortisol excess. Which condition causes this constellation and its associated secondary hypertension?

explanation.summary: Chronic glucocorticoid excess (Cushing syndrome) produces moon face, buffalo hump, central obesity with striae, thin skin, proximal myopathy, and osteoporosis; excess cortisol also raises blood pressure, causing secondary hypertension.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chronic glucocorticoid excess (Cushing syndrome) produces moon face, buffalo hump, central obesity with striae, thin skin, proximal myopathy, and osteoporosis; excess cortisol also raises blood pressure, causing secondary hypertension.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Conn syndrome causes hypertension with hypokalemia and suppressed renin, but no moon facies, striae or buffalo hump.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Acromegaly causes coarse facial features, enlarged hands and feet and macroglossia from GH excess, not central obesity with striae.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Graves disease causes weight loss, tremor, goiter and exophthalmos, with systolic hypertension from high output, not central fat redistribution.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Addison disease is cortisol deficiency, causing hypotension, hyperpigmentation and weight loss, the opposite of this picture.

questions.stem: This renal artery abnormality producing a 'string of beads' and alternating stenosis is characteristic of a condition that most classically causes renovascular hypertension in which patient group?

explanation.summary: Fibromuscular dysplasia causes non-atherosclerotic thickening of the arterial wall, giving a beaded appearance with intervening stenoses. It predominantly affects young to middle-aged women and is a treatable cause of secondary hypertension.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fibromuscular dysplasia causes non-atherosclerotic thickening of the arterial wall, giving a beaded appearance with intervening stenoses. It predominantly affects young to middle-aged women and is a treatable cause of secondary hypertension.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adolescent boys are not the classic group for fibromuscular dysplasia; renal hypertension in young males more often reflects parenchymal disease or coarctation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Elderly men with diffuse atherosclerosis get ostial atherosclerotic renal stenosis, the other main renovascular cause, not a beaded artery.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Older diabetic men are prone to atherosclerotic stenosis, not to fibromuscular dysplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hypertension in neonates usually comes from umbilical artery catheter thrombosis or congenital renal disease, not fibromuscular dysplasia.

questions.stem: This sagittal illustration of a sleeping person shows the tongue and soft tissues falling back against the pharyngeal wall. What process is being depicted?

explanation.summary: During sleep, relaxation of pharyngeal muscles lets the tongue and soft palate collapse posteriorly, occluding the upper airway. This is obstructive sleep apnea, a recognized secondary cause of hypertension.
explanation.whyCorrect: During sleep, relaxation of pharyngeal muscles lets the tongue and soft palate collapse posteriorly, occluding the upper airway. This is obstructive sleep apnea, a recognized secondary cause of hypertension.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Laryngospasm is reflex closure of the vocal cords triggered by aspiration or airway irritation, not tongue and soft tissue falling back during sleep.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Epiglottitis is infectious swelling of the epiglottis with fever, drooling and stridor while awake, not a sleep-related collapse.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Choanal atresia is a congenital blockage of the posterior nasal passage that presents in newborns with cyanosis relieved by crying.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vocal cord paralysis affects the larynx, causing hoarseness or stridor, rather than collapse of the pharynx during sleep.

questions.stem: Comparing these two fundus photos: the left shows a sharp normal optic disc, while the right shows a swollen, elevated disc with blurred margins and engorged vessels. In a patient with a blood pressure of 220/130 mmHg, the finding on the right indicates what?

explanation.summary: Disc swelling with blurred margins and engorged vessels is papilledema; in the setting of severely elevated blood pressure it defines a hypertensive emergency (grade IV/malignant hypertension) requiring urgent BP lowering.
explanation.whyCorrect: Disc swelling with blurred margins and engorged vessels is papilledema; in the setting of severely elevated blood pressure it defines a hypertensive emergency (grade IV/malignant hypertension) requiring urgent BP lowering.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Retinal detachment appears as an elevated, gray, folded retina away from the disc, not a swollen optic disc with blurred margins.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glaucomatous cupping enlarges and deepens the central cup with thinning of the neuroretinal rim, the opposite of a swollen, elevated disc.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Optic atrophy produces a pale, flat disc with sharp margins, not a swollen, hyperemic one.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A normal physiologic cup sits in a flat disc with sharp margins, as in the left photo, not the swollen disc on the right.

questions.stem: This peripheral blood smear (abnormal cells circled) shows fragmented red cells with sharp points and helmet shapes. In a patient with malignant hypertension and rising creatinine, these cells indicate which process?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sickle cells from sickle cell disease

explanation.summary: Schistocytes are red cells sheared as they pass through fibrin/damaged small vessels. In malignant hypertension the microvascular injury causes a microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, evidenced by these fragmented cells on the smear.
explanation.whyCorrect: Schistocytes are red cells sheared as they pass through fibrin/damaged small vessels. In malignant hypertension the microvascular injury causes a microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, evidenced by these fragmented cells on the smear.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Spherocytes are small, round, dense cells without central pallor from a membrane defect, not fragmented cells with sharp points.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Rouleaux are red cells stacked like coins because of excess paraprotein; the cells themselves are intact.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sickle cells are elongated crescents from HbS polymerization, not helmet-shaped fragments.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Target cells have a central dark spot within a pale ring, reflecting excess membrane relative to hemoglobin, not sheared fragments.

questions.stem: This renal biopsy from a patient with severely elevated blood pressure shows an arteriole with concentric laminated 'onion-skin' wall thickening and marked luminal narrowing next to a glomerulus and tubules. This vascular lesion is characteristic of which entity?

explanation.summary: Malignant/accelerated hypertension causes hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis, with concentric onion-skin layering of smooth muscle and basement membrane that severely narrows the lumen and produces ischemic renal injury.
explanation.whyCorrect: Malignant/accelerated hypertension causes hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis, with concentric onion-skin layering of smooth muscle and basement membrane that severely narrows the lumen and produces ischemic renal injury.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Renal artery atherosclerosis affects the main renal artery with lipid plaques, not small intrarenal arterioles with laminated walls.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Membranous glomerulonephritis thickens glomerular capillary basement membranes with subepithelial deposits and does not involve arterioles.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Acute tubular necrosis injures tubular epithelial cells with casts and denuded basement membranes; vessels are spared.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Diabetic nodular glomerulosclerosis forms Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules in the mesangium, and its arteriolar change is hyaline, not onion-skin.

questions.stem: This H&E section of a small arteriole shows the vessel wall replaced by a bright eosinophilic, smudgy acellular deposit with surrounding inflammation. In a patient with a hypertensive emergency, what is the significance of this finding?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fibrinoid necrosis indicating acute severe hypertensive vascular injury

choices.label: D
choices.text: Atherosclerotic plaque with a lipid core

explanation.summary: Fibrinoid necrosis is deposition of plasma proteins and fibrin in a necrotic vessel wall and is the hallmark acute lesion of malignant hypertension, reflecting endothelial injury from abruptly, severely elevated pressures.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fibrinoid necrosis is deposition of plasma proteins and fibrin in a necrotic vessel wall and is the hallmark acute lesion of malignant hypertension, reflecting endothelial injury from abruptly, severely elevated pressures.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amyloid is acellular and eosinophilic but has a glassy, homogeneous look, stains with Congo red, and accumulates chronically without acute inflammation or necrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Benign hyaline arteriolosclerosis is a smooth, homogeneous pink thickening without necrosis or inflammation, a chronic change rather than acute injury.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Atherosclerotic plaque affects large and medium arteries, with a lipid core, foam cells and a fibrous cap, not small arterioles.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Caseating granulomas have central necrosis rimmed by epithelioid histiocytes and giant cells, typical of tuberculosis, not hypertensive vascular injury.
